title: docs: unindent @section Cache pruning so roxygen recognizes it
description:
`R/cache-mem.R` had an indented `#'   @section Cache pruning:` tag. Roxygen only treats `@section` as a tag when it is flush after `#' `, so the indented form was emitted as literal `@section Cache pruning:` text inside the Missing keys section of `man/cache_mem.Rd` instead of a real `\section{Cache pruning}`.

This PR:
- unindents the tag in `R/cache-mem.R`
- fixes `man/cache_mem.Rd` so Cache pruning is its own section

Fixes #49.

title: Use tempfile() instead of random_hex() for temp file generation in cache_disk$set()
description:
Fixes #29 

This PR changes `cache_disk$set()` so that instead of using `random_hex()` to custom generate the file names for temp files in the cache directory, it uses `tempfile()` with the `tmpdir` argument. The `random_hex()` function could be removed after this change since this was the only place that used it (but the PR does not remove it).

## Benefits

I believe this change provides a number of benefits:

- Unaffected by `set.seed()`
  - If two code paths using different caches on the same dir were to both set the same random seed before using the cache (for reproducible simulation of data for example), this could quite plausibly result in `random_hex()` returning the exact same value for both, leading to collisions. `tempfile()` is fully independent of the user-facing random seed and is therefore unaffected.
  - See a reprex at the bottom demonstrating how such a collision could occur with the current method (the `old()` in the reprex)
- Does not update user-facing random seed
  - This is the original issue #29. `tempfile()` is fully independent of the user-facing seed, so this small change fixes that issue in a much more targeted way than the previous `with_local_seed()` approach, with less chance of negative side effects (and with some positive side effects)
  - See reprex for demonstration that the seed is in fact not affected by the `new()` approach
- Is slightly faster
  - Using `tempfile()` is slightly (around 20% in my tests) faster than the old approach. Modest, but in the right direction 

## Drawbacks

I do not believe there are any drawbacks to this approach, but below are my notes on the two potential objections I managed to imagine 😊

- Preferences for the structure of the temp file names. 
  - The resulting names are almost identical in structure, except that a "./" is prepended when `file` is in the current directory and given by relative path. Semantically the preceding period is fully equivalent (the same file will be created with or without it), and in any case, in `set()` the path has already been normalized to an absolute path when this is called.
- Changing the approach to prevent conflicts does carry the minuscule chance that some new edge case is introduced, but this should be mitigated by the fact that this is exactly the purpose of `tempfile()`
  - There is a cryptic note in `tmpfile()` help that "The names are very likely to be unique among calls to tempfile in an R session and across simultaneous R sessions (unless tmpdir is specified)". This is however contradicted by the note on parallel processing in the same help entry, which says that parallel processes "share a per-session temporary directory ... This is circumvented by ensuring that tempfile calls in different children try different names."
  - My testing has demonstrated that it _is_ indeed the case that each new process gets a unique prefix – presumably exactly to ensure that two processes should never be able to conflict.
  - Out of an abundance of caution, this fix includes the per-process unique part of the temp dir `basename(tempdir())` part as well as the standard tempfile string, giving exactly the same protections against conflicts as using the default temp dir.

## Reprex

Below is a reprex that demonstrates several aspects of this small change:

``` r
# Example paths and function stubs for old and new approach
files <- c("x.rds", "cachem/x.rds", "../cachem/x.rds", "/tmp/cachem/x.rds")
old <- function(file) {
  paste0(file, "-temp-", cachem:::random_hex(16))
}
new <- function(file) {
  tempfile(paste0(basename(file), "-temp-", basename(tempdir())), tmpdir = dirname(file))
}


## Compatibility

# Output has the exact same structure, except for current dir, were it
# gets prefixed with './', which is semantically equivalent.
tibble::tibble(
  old  = sapply(files, old),
  new  = sapply(files, new)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   old                                     new                                   
#>   <chr>                                   <chr>                                 
#> 1 x.rds-temp-6ec1e6308bdbedf5             ./x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd12127400e  
#> 2 cachem/x.rds-temp-af7174d952e89d7c      cachem/x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd117de…
#> 3 ../cachem/x.rds-temp-97958b5fb8151b53   ../cachem/x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd1a…
#> 4 /tmp/cachem/x.rds-temp-dcea9e4c9bcdf8c2 /tmp/cachem/x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd…


## Speed

# New approach is slightly faster (around 20%)
bm <- bench::mark(
  old  = sapply(files, old),
  new  = sapply(files, new),
  check = FALSE
)
bm |> dplyr::select(expression:mem_alloc)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
#> 1 old          25.1µs   28.9µs    33531.        0B
#> 2 new          19.1µs   21.1µs    45961.        0B


## Impact of seed on the set() function

# Old: File name is duplicated if seed is deterministic
set.seed(42)
old("x.rds")
#> [1] "x.rds-temp-040893190fe76384"
set.seed(42)
old("x.rds")
#> [1] "x.rds-temp-040893190fe76384"

# New: File name is never duplicated, as tempfile() is
# unaffected by the seed
set.seed(42)
new("x.rds")
#> [1] "./x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd1261d86db"
set.seed(42)
new("x.rds")
#> [1] "./x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd15c80a769"


## Impact of set() function on the seed

# Helper: True if seed was freshly set to 42
seed_is_fresh <- function() {
  sample.int(11111, 1) == 10801
}
set.seed(42)
seed_is_fresh()
#> [1] TRUE

# Old: Calling modifies shared random seed
set.seed(42)
old("x.rds")
#> [1] "x.rds-temp-040893190fe76384"
seed_is_fresh()
#> [1] FALSE

# New: Using tempfile() does not touch shared random seed
set.seed(42)
new("x.rds")
#> [1] "./x.rds-temp-Rtmpufprk116bd126f0df1"
seed_is_fresh()
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: Fix cache_layered() search error when a layer uses a custom `missing`
description:
- Fixes #26
- Formally independent of recent PR #55 (but see note at the bottom)

## Symptom

```r
m1 <- cache_mem(missing = NULL)   # fast layer
m2 <- cache_mem()                 # slow layer
cl <- cache_layered(m1, m2)
m2$set("a", 100)

cl$get("a")   #> NULL      m2 is never searched
```

## Cause

`get()` decides hit-vs-miss with `is.key_missing(value)`, but `value` is whatever that layer's own `missing` produced, and the API lets the user configure it per cache.

## Fix

```diff
-      value <- caches[[i]]$get(key)
+      value <- caches[[i]]$get(key, missing = key_missing())
```

This hard codes using `key_missing()` for the underlying caches, while allowing the user to customize what the layered cache does on a true cache miss.

It is worth noting that two things share the name `missing`: what the caller gets back when no layer has the key, and how a layer signals "I don't have it". Only the first can be configurable, but if sane behavior of layered caches is to be maintained, the second must be an unambiguous sentinel. The layered cache's own `missing` is still honoured, evaluated once at the end.

## Also in this PR

Small things needed to make that coherent:

- `cache_layered()` and its `$get()` gain a `missing` argument, matching `cache_mem()` and `cache_disk()`. Previously the value returned on a miss was whichever one belonged to the last layer, and couldn't be overridden per call. With no layers at all, `$get()` returned the loop initialiser, `NULL`.
- `$keys()` returns `character(0)`, not `NULL`, when there are no layers.

## Tests

`cache_layered()` had no test file. This adds one, including both the failure modes above, and other baseline tests that should pass for layered caches. The failure mode tests would fail, of course, before applying the fix. All tests pass after the fix has been applied.

## Note on PR #55 

This branch has no code conflicts with #55 (fixing issue with assigning `NULL` to a `cache_mem()`). I would, however, recommend applying that PR before this one, because that issue with strange behavior under `NULL` assignment would propagate to layered caches (and because that PR addresses a data corruption issue with a non-experimental cache type, whereas this deals only with an experimental (but very useful) type).

title: Fix cache_mem corruption when storing a NULL value
description:
This fixes issue #54 

## Symptom

```r
m <- cache_mem()
m$set("a", 1); m$set("b", 2); m$set("c", 3); m$set("d", 4)
m$set("b", NULL)

m$get("b")   #> 3      wrong
m$get("c")   #> 4      wrong
m$get("d")   #> NULL   wrong
```

Every key stored after the `NULL` returns the next key's value. 

## Cause

`set()` uses `value_[[new_idx]] <<- value`. On a list, `[[<-` with a `NULL` RHS deletes the element and shifts the rest down, while `key_idx_map_` keeps pointing at the old indices.

## Fix

```diff
-    value_[[new_idx]] <<- value
+    value_[new_idx]   <<- list(value)

-        value_[[last_idx_]] <<- value_[[idx]]
+        value_[last_idx_]   <<- value_[idx]
```

## Why this does not introduce other regressions

`x[i] <- x[j]` and `x[[i]] <- x[[j]]` on a list differ only when the value is `NULL`. For all other values, assigning a sliced list of length 1 that containing an object to another slice of length 1 is equivalent to assigning the object itself to that place in the list. 

## Tests

The PR contains a number of tests that verify the fix. One set of tests verifies the expected behavior explicitly. The other set compares `cache_mem()` behavior with `cache_disk()`. Both of these tests fail before implementing the fix but pass after implementing it. All other tests pass after implementing the fix.

title: Add "Supported By Posit" badge to cachem website
description:
## Overview

This PR adds the "Supported by Posit" badge to the cachem website.

## Background

We've recently started adding a "Supported by Posit" badge across all Posit package websites to create a more cohesive brand presence. The badge appears on the far right of the top navigation bar or at the bottom of the hamburger menu. It links to Posit’s main website. @hadley is involved with this initiative.

The following websites already have the "Supported by Posit" badge: [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org), [Great Tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/articles/intro.html), [gt](https://gt.rstudio.com), [Plotnine](https://plotnine.org), [Pointblank](https://posit-dev.github.io/pointblank/), [pointblank](https://rstudio.github.io/pointblank/), and [Quarto](https://quarto.org).

See https://posit-dev.github.io/supported-by-posit/ for more information.

## Changes

- Added a line to `_pkgdown.yml` to include the JavaScript file
- Standardized indentation in `_pkgdown.yml`

title: Fix spurious `nothing to compact` message
description:
Closes #47.

Prior to this change, the internal cache objects could shrink smaller than `INITIAL_SIZE` or `COMPACT_LIMIT`. This PR:

- Removes `COMPACT_LIMIT` and just uses `INITIAL_SIZE` as the minimum size.
- Makes it so the storage vectors won't shrink smaller than `INITIAL_SIZE`.

This makes it so the `nothing to compact` message won't show up anymore.

This also requires the development version of fastmap, from after https://github.com/r-lib/fastmap/pull/39 was merged.

title: fix #34, add 'ttl' method to mem and disk caches
Add support for custom serialization functions to disk
description:
This generalizes the reading and writing to allows users to use other
methods of serializing objects to disk.

This may be beneficial if the default methods of `readRDS` and `saveRDS`
are too slow, or if the users want to change the amount of compression
used. It also allows the use of faster serialization methods like fst.

Or for specialized cases where you are always caching one type of object
(like data frames) you can use object specific formats like parquet
files.

title: Make sure cache objects don't affect RNG state
description:
Closes #29. I based this implementation on Shiny's `withPrivateSeed()` function: https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/blob/78d77ce37/R/utils.R#L54-L88

The one thing I didn't bring over was the call to `httpuv::getRNGState()`, which was needed because of https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/issues/1763. We probably need something like this in cases where an Rcpp function (in C++) calls this R code, though I don't know for sure right now.. If we implement this, we'll want to do it without bringing in an httpuv dependency or even Rcpp -- we'll want to implement it with C in the src/ directory.

title: Show proper default value for `max_age` param to `cache_mem()`
description:
`cache_mem()` has been inheriting parameter documentation from `cache_disk()`, however the default value for the `max_age` parameter differs between the two.

This adds explicit documentation for `cache_mem()`'s version of the parameter with the correct 512 MB default value.

title: Faster pruning
description:
This PR does the following to `cache_mem`:

* It only attempts pruning (after each call to `$set()` if `max_n`, `max_size` are exceeded, or if there is a non-default value for `max_age`. This greatly improves performance in normal use cases when the cache isn't full.
* It uses data structures that are faster for finding which which items should be pruned.

title: Faster prune for cache_mem
description:
Closes #4. This speeds up the pruning for `cache_mem()`.

It may be possible to have even faster pruning in the future, but it will probably require new data structures to store the metadata.
